note: Extracted 14 September 2026 from fourteen CC BY 4.0 articles, each licence read in the retrieved full text, with no text-and-data-mining or AI restriction found. OpenStax is excluded (D-26). Not used: two passages on the occupancy equation from a lower-selectivity venue; an opioid-specific, largely preclinical account of pharmacokinetic tolerance; and a structural review that discloses an AI-drafted summary. The selectivity statements come from anaesthetic pharmacology and carry that label; a published comment on that article was not read. Every quote was checked word for word.

topic.title: Receptors, agonists and antagonists (English sources)
topic.publicationChapter: Understanding Peptides — Five: Receptors; Peptide Science & Applications — Four: Receptors, signalling and modulation
topic.summary: Kinds of drug target; binding as the basis of action; affinity and efficacy and why they cannot simply be measured apart; full, partial and inverse agonists; antagonists; spare receptors; constitutive activity; biased agonism; allosteric modulation; desensitisation, tachyphylaxis and tolerance; and why selectivity is relative. Corroborates, and in one place qualifies, the claims read from the Spanish sample of Rang and Dale.
topic.notes: Tolerance from mediator depletion, a clean definition of surmountable competitive antagonism, and a statement that most peptide hormones act through GPCRs are not in any permissive source held.

claims.claimText: Alexander et al. (2025, Concise Guide to PHARMACOLOGY) group human drug targets into GPCRs, ion channels, catalytic receptors, nuclear hormone receptors, enzymes, transporters and other protein targets.
claims.plainLanguageText: Drugs act on a handful of broad kinds of protein target, and receptors are only one of them.
claims.interpretationNotes: Classification scheme of a curated guide; says nothing about how often each class is targeted.
claims.uncertaintyText: General receptor pharmacology from peer-reviewed English-language sources. Several illustrate a principle with one drug class; applying the principle to peptides is an extrapolation and is labelled as one. Nothing here says which receptor any peptide acts on.

evidence.interpretation: Classification scheme of a curated guide; says nothing about how often each class is targeted.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: The review's own statement, with no citation attached; nothing behind it can be traced.

claims.claimText: Watts et al. (2023 review) state that drug action rests on a drug binding to, i.e. having affinity for, its target.
claims.plainLanguageText: A molecule has to attach to its target before it can do anything there.
claims.interpretationNotes: Review-level principle; the same passage lists covalent/irreversible binding among binding types.
claims.uncertaintyText: General receptor pharmacology from peer-reviewed English-language sources. Several illustrate a principle with one drug class; applying the principle to peptides is an extrapolation and is labelled as one. Nothing here says which receptor any peptide acts on.

evidence.interpretation: Review-level principle; the same passage lists covalent/irreversible binding among binding types.
evidence.primaryTraceNote: A review. The primary studies it cites have not been obtained and read by this index.

claims.claimText: Liu et al. (2024 review) describe affinity as how tightly a drug binds its receptor and efficacy as how effectively the drug–receptor complex promotes a physiological response.
claims.plainLanguageText: Sticking to a receptor and switching it on are two different properties.
claims.interpretationNotes: Historical framing (1950s receptor theory). Pair with REC-06, which qualifies whether the two can be measured separately.
claims.uncertaintyText: General receptor pharmacology from peer-reviewed English-language sources. Several illustrate a principle with one drug class; applying the principle to peptides is an extrapolation and is labelled as one. Nothing here says which receptor any peptide acts on.

claims.claimText: Watts et al. define a full agonist as giving a full response in a system, and partial agonists as producing less than the full agonist's response.
claims.plainLanguageText: Some molecules switch a receptor fully on; others only partly, even when bound.
claims.interpretationNotes: Definition is relative to 'a system'; maximal response depends on tissue/assay.
claims.uncertaintyText: General receptor pharmacology from peer-reviewed English-language sources. Several illustrate a principle with one drug class; applying the principle to peptides is an extrapolation and is labelled as one. Nothing here says which receptor any peptide acts on.

claims.claimText: Watts et al. describe antagonists as lacking the ability to activate a receptor while blocking activation by agonists.
claims.plainLanguageText: A blocker sits on the receptor without switching it on, which stops activators from working.
claims.interpretationNotes: Does not distinguish competitive, irreversible and non-competitive mechanisms (see REC-15, REC-19 and coverage).

claims.claimText: Higham and Colquhoun (2024) show, using a two-step binding–activation mechanism, that measured agonist binding depends on efficacy as well as microscopic affinity.
claims.plainLanguageText: How strongly an activating molecule seems to bind is partly shaped by how well it switches the receptor on, so the two can't simply be read off separately.
claims.interpretationNotes: Qualifies a simple 'binding then activation as independent steps' framing: conceptually distinct steps, but not separable from equilibrium binding/response data alone. Theoretical argument (del Castillo–Katz scheme).
claims.uncertaintyText: General receptor pharmacology from peer-reviewed English-language sources. Several illustrate a principle with one drug class; applying the principle to peptides is an extrapolation and is labelled as one. Nothing here says which receptor any peptide acts on.

claims.claimText: Higham and Colquhoun explain that when a response is limited by factors other than receptor saturation, a maximal response may come from activating a small fraction of receptors, which are then termed spare receptors.
claims.plainLanguageText: Sometimes a cell gives its full response when only a few of its receptors are switched on; the rest are called 'spare'.
claims.interpretationNotes: Illustrated with the muscle endplate (ion channels); 'spare' reflects the response system, not a special receptor type.
claims.uncertaintyText: General receptor pharmacology from peer-reviewed English-language sources. Several illustrate a principle with one drug class; applying the principle to peptides is an extrapolation and is labelled as one. Nothing here says which receptor any peptide acts on.

claims.plainLanguageText: Receptor reserve is the share of receptors a full activator doesn't need to produce its biggest effect.
claims.interpretationNotes: Adenosine-receptor review; general definition only. Corroborates REC-09.

claims.interpretationNotes: Says 'several GPCRs', not all receptors.

claims.plainLanguageText: Some 'blockers' actually turn down a receptor's background activity, not just stop activators.
claims.interpretationNotes: The paper stresses that measured inverse agonism depends on the experimental system (high expression / constitutively active mutants).

claims.claimText: Michel et al. state that measured inverse agonism depends partly on the experimental model, so one compound may appear as a partial agonist, neutral antagonist or inverse agonist in different models.
claims.plainLanguageText: The same molecule can look like an activator, a blocker or a 'turner-down' depending on where it is tested.
claims.interpretationNotes: Caveat against treating ligand labels as fixed; based on adrenoceptor literature.

claims.interpretationNotes: Same section notes 'probe dependence': effects can differ with the orthosteric ligand bound.

claims.interpretationNotes: Described for beta-adrenergic receptors as the GPCR prototype; elsewhere the review attributes desensitisation to kinase phosphorylation, beta-arrestin recruitment and internalisation.

claims.claimText: Allouche et al. (2014) define receptor desensitisation as reduced signalling after acute agonist activation that recovers in agonist-free conditions, distinguishing it from tolerance.
claims.plainLanguageText: Desensitisation is a short-term dulling of the receptor signal that recovers once the drug is removed.
claims.interpretationNotes: Opioid-receptor (OR) wording; same passage defines tolerance as 'a decrease of the drug response' with chronic use and describes cellular tolerance not reversing within hours.

notYetSupported.statement: That most peptide hormones act through G-protein-coupled receptors.
notYetSupported.why: The nomenclature guide states that one GPCR family binds polypeptide hormones and that class A includes peptide receptors; no permissive source held states the general proportion.
notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A permissively licensed source stating it.

notYetSupported.statement: Tolerance arising from depletion of a mediator, and a definition of competitive antagonism as surmountable.

notYetSupported.whatWouldResolveIt: A permissively licensed pharmacology review covering them.
